prompt: Put the parts of Lívia's ten minutes in Minto's order.
items: Friday evening is our busiest three hours
A growing share of checkouts fail, and on 6 March it stopped
Six engineer-weeks and R$ 4,000 a month; approve it today

prompt: How can Lívia check that her complication is really a complication?

choices.text: It makes the audience ask "so what do we do?"
choices.why: Right: if it does not raise that question, it is more situation.

choices.text: Everybody in the room already agrees with it
choices.why: That is the test for the situation, not the complication.

choices.text: It is the longest part of the presentation, so the tension has time to build
choices.why: Length is not the test.

choices.text: It contains at least one number from the logs
choices.why: Numbers help, but a number can be pure situation too.

prompt: Situation-complication-resolution seems to contradict lesson 1's "answer first". How does Lívia reconcile them?
hint: What she says in the first thirty seconds.

choices.text: She shows the resolution slide first and skips the story
choices.why: The story is what earns the resolution.

choices.text: She announces the ask, then tells the story
choices.why: Right: the resolution is announced, then earned.

choices.text: She tells the story and saves the ask for a follow-up email
choices.why: Then the meeting ends without a decision.

choices.text: She drops the answer-first rule for presentations, which are a different medium
choices.why: She keeps it: the resolution is announced first.

prompt: Lívia's investigation found eleven things worth knowing; nine are not in the presentation. Why?
hint: What does each fact do to the audience's path?

choices.text: There was no time to put them on slides
choices.why: It was a choice, not a shortage.

choices.text: None changes the decision, so each one makes it harder to reach
choices.why: Right: they wait in the appendix for anybody who asks.

choices.text: The audience is not technical enough to follow them
choices.why: The test is whether they move the decision, not the audience's capacity.

choices.text: They were not true enough to present
choices.why: The lesson says they are true and interesting.

prompt: Why does a presentation organised around technologies give a leadership audience nothing to decide?

choices.text: Only the CTO may approve a technology choice
choices.why: Marola's decision went to Renata and Caio, and the lesson's point is broader than who signs.

choices.text: They approve an outcome at a price, not a method
choices.why: Right: technologies are the method.

choices.text: Technologies change too fast to be decided in a meeting
choices.why: Speed of change is not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: Leaders find technology boring
choices.why: Interest is not the issue; the unit of the decision is.

prompt: The lesson names a "less comfortable reason" presenters fill decks with technology slides. What is it?
hint: Nobody can disagree with how replication works.

choices.text: They take less time to prepare than charts
choices.why: Effort is not the reason named.

choices.text: Vendors supply them ready-made, logos included
choices.why: Not in the lesson.

choices.text: They are safe: nobody objects, and nothing gets decided
choices.why: Right: a decision slide invites disagreement, which is its point.

choices.text: Leaders ask for them to check that engineers know their tools
choices.why: Nothing suggests the audience asked for them.

prompt: Where may a technology appear in a decision presentation, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: As the answer to a question somebody asks
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: As a diagram of logos showing the current architecture
choices.why: That is slide 1 of the draft the lesson rewrote.

choices.text: As the title of the opening slide
choices.why: The opening carries the ask.

choices.text: As the name of a priced option
choices.why: Yes: "a larger database server, R$ 9,000 a month".

prompt: Which question from Bruna turned the first outline into the second?
hint: It is about the end of the meeting.

choices.text: "How long is your slot?"
choices.why: Useful, but not the question that changed the outline.

choices.text: "What do you want them to say at the end?"
choices.why: Right: it forces the decision to the centre.

choices.text: "Have you shown the replication mode?"
choices.why: That would have added a technology slide.

choices.text: "Is there a slide with the full architecture and every component?"
choices.why: That is the trap, not the way out.

prompt: Which slide title follows the assertion-evidence structure?

choices.text: Every option but doing nothing costs less than a year of losses
choices.why: Right: the title is the claim, and the chart below is its evidence.

choices.text: Options
choices.why: A topic, not a claim.

choices.text: Options: a comparison
choices.why: A topic with a subtitle.

choices.text: Options considered for the database problem
choices.why: Longer, and still a topic.

prompt: Why does the lesson keep text on slides to a minimum?

choices.text: Text cannot be translated for the Portuguese audience
choices.why: Translation is not the issue.

choices.text: Slides with text look unprofessional to leadership
choices.why: Appearance is not the argument; attention is.

choices.text: The audience reads ahead, then stops listening
choices.why: Right: text on a slide competes with the presenter.

choices.text: Projectors cannot render small fonts legibly
choices.why: A practical point, not the one made.

prompt: Which of these are among the smaller rules in the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Number the slides
choices.why: Yes: so a question can say "on slide 4".

choices.text: Delete the agenda slide in a short talk
choices.why: Yes: the first thirty seconds do its job.

choices.text: Show the date and source under a chart
choices.why: Yes: Caio will ask.

choices.text: Read each slide aloud so nobody misses it
choices.why: The opposite: do not read the slide.

prompt: When the claim is a number, the lesson suggests showing one ___ number on an empty slide.
Why does Lívia write down the three hardest questions before the meeting?

choices.text: To steer the meeting so those questions never come up
choices.why: The aim is to answer them well, not to avoid them.

choices.text: To put them on a final slide called "FAQ" so nobody needs to ask them aloud
choices.why: That would shut down the questions where the decision is made.

choices.text: To hand them to a colleague to answer
choices.why: She answers them herself.

choices.text: An answer given once already comes out calm, not defensive
choices.why: Right: the preparation matters more than the answers.

prompt: Put the steps for taking a question in the lesson's order.
items: Restate the question in one sentence

prompt: Caio asks something Lívia cannot answer on the spot. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Give her best estimate confidently so the meeting keeps its momentum
choices.why: A guess that turns out wrong discredits everything else she said.

choices.text: Move on to the next slide and hope it is forgotten
choices.why: It is not forgotten.

choices.text: Ask Bruna to answer instead
choices.why: Possible if Bruna knows; the lesson's point is that "I don't know" is an answer.

choices.text: Say she does not know, and when she will
choices.why: Right: and write it down where he can see, then keep the promise.

prompt: Renata objects: "April is when we promised the substitution flow." What did Lívia do?

choices.text: Offered to delay the replica until June to keep the peace
choices.why: That gives up the decision without addressing the concern.

choices.text: Asked Otávio to overrule her
choices.why: Escalating in the room turns an objection into a conflict.

choices.text: Offered to join the call where Renata tells the stores
choices.why: Right: the concern was a promise Renata would have to move.

choices.text: Repeated the case for the replica, more firmly
choices.why: The objection was not about the replica.

prompt: What is the purpose of Lívia's twenty-minute conversations before 19 March?
hint: Where changing a view costs nothing.

choices.text: To replace the meeting, which is then cancelled
choices.why: The meeting still happens and makes the decision.

choices.text: To find out who will vote against her so she can avoid inviting them
choices.why: Nobody votes, and nobody is left out.

choices.text: To let each decider object privately
choices.why: Right: and to change the proposal before it is a public position.

choices.text: To lobby each decider until they promise a yes
choices.why: The lesson says none of them was a sales pitch.

prompt: Lívia's ten-minute slot held a version that took how many minutes when she first said it aloud?
On a video call, why does Lívia ask "Caio, does the cost work for you?" instead of "any questions?"
hint: What silence means on a call.

choices.text: On a call, silence means nothing
choices.why: Right: a named question is a question; "any questions?" is a pause.

choices.text: To stop anybody else from speaking
choices.why: The others can still speak; the named question just gets an answer.

choices.text: Caio is the most senior person on the call
choices.why: Otávio is; seniority is not the reason.

choices.text: Naming people is more polite on video
choices.why: Politeness is not the point.

prompt: A team lead shares a document on screen for the first time and talks through it while the room reads. What goes wrong, by lessons 2 and 5?

choices.text: They read and do not listen
choices.why: Right: either send it before, or read it together in silence first.

choices.text: Nothing, if the document is short and well written
choices.why: Even a short document competes with the voice.

choices.text: The decision is made too quickly to be safe
choices.why: The usual outcome is the opposite: no decision.

choices.text: The document leaks to people outside the meeting
choices.why: Not the failure the lessons describe.
